segments.narration_text:
November 2008. Nariman House, Mumbai. Two gunmen are holding a Jewish centre, and commandos are about to come down the stairs. On a phone line from Pakistan, a calm voice gives them an order. Pile the mattresses at the top of the stairs. Wait for the commandos.

Six hostages died in that building. Among them were a rabbi and his wife. Later, according to court testimony, a friend of the plotters compared the man on the phone to one of history's great generals. The compliment was passed along to him.

The man on the phone was never in the room. His name is Sajid Mir, and the FBI calls him the chief planner of 26/11. Since then, Pakistan has described him as free, as dead, and — for one very convenient season — as a convict. So where is the man who ran Mumbai by phone? And why has no court ever tried him for it?

Everything here comes from the FBI's wanted notice, sworn testimony in a Chicago courtroom, and Pakistan's own court order. His status, it turns out, changes whenever someone needs it to.

paragraphs.text: He didn't need to hide, either. Zabiuddin Ansari, a Lashkar operative later arrested by India, told investigators that Mir twice visited Zaki-ur-Rehman Lakhvi in Adiala Jail, in Rawalpindi. Then someone started asking who mattered.

The Financial Action Task Force is the global watchdog on terror financing. It had kept Pakistan on its grey list since 2018, and its next key review was due in Berlin in June 2022.

In April 2022, the dead man was arrested. Weeks later, on May 16, an anti-terrorism court convicted him. Not for Mumbai. For financing terrorism. Fifteen and a half years, across three sentences. The trial was held behind closed doors, inside Lahore's Kot Lakhpat Jail. No reporters. No announcement. According to Dawn, the verdict surfaced only weeks later, through court papers and lawyers.

Pakistan put the conviction in front of the watchdog. It worked. That October, Pakistan came off the grey list.

Dead while nobody was asking. Alive, arrested and convicted in the weeks a regulator needed proof. And never once tried for the attack that killed 166 people.

Mir had been poisoned inside Dera Ghazi Khan Central Jail, they said, and flown by the army to a military hospital in Bahawalpur, on a ventilator. None of it has been confirmed. Indian intelligence sources suggested, without proof, that it might have been staged — a way to vanish before anyone could ask for him again.

paragraphs.text: Every other name in this story ended on the record. Headley took a plea. Rana was extradited to face trial. Sajid Mir's record does something else. It opens and closes on command. Dead when that was convenient. Convicted when a regulator needed proof. Tried only for a crime that never required saying the word Mumbai in open court.
